common_name: McDonald Hazelnut (OSU 880.027, Eastern Filbert Blight-Resistant Peeling Filbert)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container hazelnuts in late winter or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; McDonald is self-incompatible and requires a compatible cross-pollinating companion variety; released by Oregon State University in 2014, McDonald carries strong resistance to Eastern Filbert Blight and is recommended for the Willamette Valley and similarly humid, EFB-prone hazelnut-growing regions.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; McDonald requires a compatible pollenizer variety; nuts drop naturally when ripe, typically about 14 days earlier than the older standard 'Barcelona,' allowing growers to complete harvest before Willamette Valley autumn rains begin, which lowers drying and cleaning costs. McDonald was developed within Oregon State University's hazelnut breeding program and tested under the designation OSU 880.027, a cross of 'Tonda Pacifica' and 'Santiam,' before being released and patented in January 2014. The tree is a vigorous, heavy producer of medium-small, high-quality kernels prized for the peeled hazelnut market, with an excellent shelled-nut recovery around 52%, and it carries strong resistance to Eastern Filbert Blight, the canker disease that devastated older 'Barcelona' plantings across the Pacific Northwest.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container hazelnuts in late winter or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Daviana is grown primarily as a pollenizer for other cultivars rather than for its own nut crop; it is highly susceptible to Eastern Filbert Blight and is not recommended east of the Mississippi or in other EFB-endemic regions.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Daviana is planted primarily as a companion pollenizer rather than for nut production, since its own nut quality is considered mediocre; its catkins shed pollen later in the season than most commercial cultivars, making it a useful match for cultivars with a later-receptive bloom window. Daviana originated in England and became, historically, the most widely planted pollenizer in 'Barcelona' hazelnut orchards in the Pacific Northwest and Europe. Its high susceptibility to Eastern Filbert Blight and unremarkable nut quality have caused it to be steadily replaced by EFB-resistant pollenizers in modern commercial plantings, though it remains of interest to home orchardists in EFB-free regions.

common_name: Tonda Gentile Romana Hazelnut (Tonda Romana, Nocciola Romana DOP Filbert)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container hazelnuts in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tonda Gentile Romana is self-incompatible and requires a compatible cross-pollinating companion variety such as 'Tonda di Giffoni'; historically grown on the volcanic soils of the Cimini Mountains north of Rome, it performs best in warm-summer Mediterranean-type climates.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tonda Gentile Romana requires a compatible pollenizer; nuts ripen from late August to late September and are collected from the ground as they fall, with fine, thin shells that split easily during processing. Tonda Gentile Romana (also called Tonda Romana) is one of the principal cultivars behind the Nocciola Romana DOP, an Italian Protected Designation of Origin hazelnut grown chiefly in the province of Viterbo and parts of Rome in the Lazio region, with cultivation dating back to at least the 15th century. The nuts are small, round, with pale, delicately flavored kernels, and the cultivar is prized in the Italian confectionery industry for chocolate and traditional sweets.

common_name: Negret Hazelnut (Avellana de Reus DO Filbert, Catalan Hazelnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container hazelnuts in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Negret is self-incompatible and requires a compatible cross-pollinating companion variety, and it is prone to iron chlorosis on high-pH, calcareous soils.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Negret requires a compatible pollenizer and benefits from monitoring for iron chlorosis on alkaline soils; the tree is naturally low-vigor with a spreading, suckering habit and bears relatively late in its establishment compared to other commercial cultivars. Negret is the dominant hazelnut cultivar of Spain, accounting for roughly 70% of Spanish commercial hazelnut orchards, and is the principal variety behind the 'Avellana de Reus' Designation of Origin in the Tarragona province of Catalonia. The kernels are highly regarded by the confectionery and kernel-roasting market for their flavor and processing qualities.
sources: IRTA (Institut de Recerca i Tecnologia Agroalimentàries)
Genetic Diversity of Hazelnut Germplasm in Northeastern Spain

common_name: Buccaneer Walnut (Dutch Blight-Resistant Self-Fertile Persian Walnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Buccaneer is self-fertile and will set a crop without a companion pollenizer; it is late-leafing, which helps it avoid damage from late spring frosts, and it carries good resistance to walnut blight.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Buccaneer is self-fertile and produces heavy yields of high-quality nuts from a relatively young age (typically 4-5 years); its late-leafing habit protects the developing catkins and foliage from late spring frost damage, and it shows excellent resistance to walnut blight, a bacterial disease that can be serious in cooler, damper walnut-growing regions such as the UK and parts of northern Europe. Buccaneer originated in the Netherlands as a robust, disease-resistant Persian walnut selection bred for reliability outside the classic Mediterranean and Californian walnut belts, forming a broad-canopied tree valued both for nut production and wildlife value.

common_name: Vina Walnut (Early-Harvest Heirloom California Persian Walnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile loam or sandy loam in full sun; Vina benefits from cross-pollination with a compatible companion variety; it requires substantial winter chill and is best adapted to California's Central Valley and similar zone 7-9 climates.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Vina benefits from a compatible pollenizer for best nut set; the nuts mature and are ready for harvest roughly two weeks earlier than the widely planted 'Chandler,' making it useful where an earlier harvest window is desirable. Vina is an older, unpatented California-bred Persian walnut cultivar that predates modern UC Davis releases such as 'Chandler,' 'Howard,' 'Sunland,' 'Tulare,' and 'Solano.' It was historically grown in California's Central Valley walnut industry and has served as a reference cultivar in University of California walnut research, and remains of interest to heirloom orchardists for its earlier ripening and long production history.
sources: University of California, Davis Walnut Improvement Program
